intro.html: Put in- in front of a word and you often get its opposite: correct and incorrect, visible and invisible. All ten words in this topic are built that way. Each one is a no: impeccable is not able to go wrong, insatiable is not able to be filled up, irrevocable is not able to be called back.

in- = not. To be easier to say, it changes its last letter to match the sound after it: im- before b, m and p (impeccable), il- before l (illegal) and ir- before r (irrevocable). Many of these words end in -able or -ible, so they mean not able to be…

Peel off the in- and look at what is left. Sometimes it is a word you know (correct, apt); sometimes it is a Latin word worth learning (satis, enough; nocere, to harm). The memory hooks below lean on those parts.

words.def: perfect; without a single flaw or fault
words.ex: Her {impeccable} handwriting made the party invitations look printed.
words.ctx: The young chef’s knife work was {impeccable}: every slice of carrot was the same thickness, and not one piece was wasted.
words.etym: From Latin impeccabilis, “not able to sin”: in- (not) + peccare (to sin).

mn.cue: not a crumb to PECK: im-PECK-able
mn.text: The hen hunts all over Nana Lou’s kitchen floor and finds not one crumb to peck: the floor is {impeccable}.

scene.alt: A hen searches a spotless kitchen floor and finds nothing to peck, while a proud grandmother looks on.

words.def: clumsy; lacking the skill to do something well
words.ex: The {inept} referee kept losing track of the score.
words.ctx: Although Marcus was a gifted singer, he was {inept} at dancing; he stepped on his partner’s feet twice in the first minute.
words.etym: From Latin ineptus, “unsuited, foolish”: in- (not) + aptus (fit, apt).

mn.text: Felix is not apt at juggling: every ball he tosses ends up on the grass. He is {inept}.

scene.alt: A man tries to juggle and drops every ball while a girl laughs.

words.def: not moving or acting; without energy or force
words.ex: The cat lay {inert} on the warm windowsill all afternoon.
words.ctx: The robot had worked for hours, but once its battery ran down it sat {inert} in the corner, not stirring even when the children called its name.
words.etym: From Latin iners, “unskilled, idle”: in- (without) + ars (skill, art).
words.note: Chemists call a substance inert when it does not react with others; helium is an inert gas.

mn.text: The puppy barks and barks at the big rock lying in the dirt, but the rock never moves: it is {inert}.

scene.alt: A puppy barks at a big rock in the dirt, but the rock does not move.

words.def: impossible to defeat, tame or discourage
words.ex: The {indomitable} little team kept playing hard even when it was losing by twenty points.
words.ctx: Storms knocked down her fence three summers in a row, but Granny Mae’s spirit was {indomitable}; each time, she simply built it again, a little stronger.
words.etym: From Late Latin indomitabilis, “not able to be tamed”: in- (not) + domitare (to tame).

mn.text: Big Sven pulls with all his might, but he can’t dominate little Zoe in tug-of-war; she won’t budge an inch. She is {indomitable}.

scene.alt: A small girl holds firm in a tug-of-war against a big man, who is sweating.

words.def: impossible to stop or change; not moved by pleading
words.ex: The {inexorable} tide crept up the beach and swallowed our sandcastle.
words.ctx: We begged the clock to slow down before the last bell, but time was {inexorable}; the minutes ticked by at the same steady pace no matter what we wanted.
words.etym: From Latin inexorabilis, “not to be moved by pleading”: in- (not) + exorare (to win over by pleading).

mn.text: Pip shouts “Stop!” at the sea, but the tide keeps coming in, no exceptions: it is {inexorable}.

scene.alt: A boy holds up his hands and shouts at a big wave rolling toward his sandcastle.

words.def: impossible to satisfy; always wanting more
words.ex: The puppy had an {insatiable} appetite for tennis balls.
words.ctx: Lila’s curiosity was {insatiable}; after reading every book about volcanoes in the school library, she asked the librarian to order more.
words.etym: From Latin insatiabilis: in- (not) + satiare (to fill, satisfy), from satis (enough).

mn.text: Ivy has eaten a whole stack of pancakes and still is not satisfied: “More!” Her appetite is {insatiable}.

scene.alt: A little girl beside a tall stack of empty plates cheers for more while the cook looks amazed.

words.def: harmless; not likely to hurt or upset anyone
words.ex: Her {innocuous} question about the weather somehow started a long argument.
words.ctx: Mom worried that the new board game would start fights, but it proved {innocuous}: the worst thing that could happen was losing a turn and having to cluck like a chicken.
words.etym: From Latin innocuus, “harmless”: in- (not) + nocere (to harm).

mn.cue: in-KNOCK-YOU-ous: it can’t KNOCK YOU over
mn.text: The huge beach ball bounces right into Theo, but it is so soft it can’t knock you over; it is {innocuous}.

scene.alt: A giant soft beach ball bounces into a toddler, who laughs.

words.def: impossible to correct or reform; always misbehaving
words.ex: Our {incorrigible} parrot still squawks at the mail carrier every single morning.
words.ctx: Teachers had tried praise, extra chores and long talks, but the class clown remained {incorrigible}, cracking jokes all the way through every test.
words.etym: From Late Latin incorrigibilis: in- (not) + corrigere (to correct).

mn.text: Farmer Jamal has told the goat “No!” a hundred times, but it still eats the socks off his line; it cannot be corrected. The goat is {incorrigible}.

scene.alt: A sneaky goat runs off with a sock while the farmer shouts at it once again.

words.def: impossible to understand or read; mysterious
words.ex: The cat stared at me with an {inscrutable} look, and I had no idea what it wanted.
words.ctx: Most players grin when they draw a good card, but Grandpa Gus’s face stayed {inscrutable}, so no one at the table could guess whether he was about to win.
words.etym: From Late Latin inscrutabilis: in- (not) + scrutari (to search, examine).

mn.text: Sami scrutinizes the cat’s face with a magnifying glass, but he still can’t tell what she is thinking: her face is {inscrutable}.

scene.alt: A boy studies a cat’s blank face through a magnifying glass and still looks puzzled.

words.def: impossible to undo or take back
words.ex: Pressing “send” felt {irrevocable}; the message was already on its way.
words.ctx: The judges explained that their decision was {irrevocable}: once a skater’s score was posted, it could not be changed or taken back for any reason.
words.etym: From Latin irrevocabilis, “not able to be called back”: in- (not) + revocare (to call back).

mn.text: Once Kai drops the letter into the mailbox, he can’t call it back, however loudly he shouts: mailing it was {irrevocable}.

scene.alt: A boy reaches toward a mailbox, shouting for the letter he just mailed to come back.

after.cap: Ten words, one prefix: take off the in- and you find the thing that cannot happen.

after.html: Watch the spelling change. Before p, in- becomes im- (impeccable, impossible); before r, it becomes ir- (irrevocable, irregular), which is why those words have a double r. Before l it becomes il- (illegal, illogical).

after.name: vo-cloze

opts.s: However hard the coach argued, the referee’s call was {irrevocable}: the goal would not count.

after.cap: Which word fits? A call that cannot be taken back is irrevocable.

items.q: In which word does in- NOT mean “not”?
items.why: Inflammable means easily set on fire, the same as flammable. Its in- means in or into. Inept, insatiable and inscrutable all use in- to mean not.

items.q: The prefix in- (not) changes its spelling before some letters. Which spelling is right?
items.why: Before r, in- becomes ir-: irrevocable, like irregular and irresponsible.

items.q: A robot whose battery has died sits perfectly still in the corner. The robot is…
items.why: Inert means not moving or acting. Inept means clumsy, but the robot is not doing anything badly; it is not doing anything at all.
False. Invaluable means priceless: worth so much that no one could put a value on it. Not every in- word means what you expect, so check the sentence.

items.q: Type the word built from in- (not) + the Latin peccare (to sin) + -able. It means flawless.
items.why: Impeccable: in- becomes im- before p, and the word means not able to do wrong, so flawless.
